🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is +0.21% (intraday, 7-year -3bp). At trading day 30 (last close) it was +0.21% against a five-campaign average of -1.45% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.63%. The 10-year is +0bp since the hike vs a +19bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 2 of 4 signals: early signs of topping).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 780bp against a five-year average of 415bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is holding: single-B -2bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.36 → 0.65 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+4bp).
  • AI Credit: CoreWeave 5Y CDS 1,064bp, 131bp under the Oct 15 record and 612bp over the June low. Its June 9.625% 2032s are at 81.3 (14.6%, -4.1pts in a month). Up the stack: Nvidia 125bp, Oracle 302bp. Neocloud stocks 1m: CRWV -30%, NBIS -26%, IREN -34% vs NVDA -5%.
  • Bank Earnings: 9 banks reported (BANC, FCF, FFBC, RNST, SBCF, TRMK, UMBF, HOPE, PB); 3 red-flagged (FCF: NPLs +17% QoQ; RNST: NCO ratio +15bp QoQ; PB: NPLs +46% QoQ). Credit deteriorating at the margin; deposit costs flat. Watch: FCF, RNST, PB.
  • Stocks: US stocks edged up modestly; fear gauge eased; Japan led overseas with +1.1%.
  • FX: Dollar slipped slightly; euro stays weak versus its recent averages; yen near 158.
  • Technicals: S&P sits above its trend lines; Nasdaq dipped just below its 50-day average.
  • Sectors: Energy and defensive sectors led the month; communications stocks fell hardest.
  • Credit/Spreads: Safer corporate bonds look calm, but the riskiest junk bonds keep getting hit.
  • Crisis: Moderate stress: high long-term rates, $100 oil and junk weakness, not panic.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is steady around its historical middle; energy prices keep headline prices hot.
  • Tech Bubble: Tech prices are well below dot-com extremes, but credit and volatility show complacency.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Watch Apple on Nov 2 and Flex, which options price for the biggest move; we could not confirm any upcoming IPO deals.
  • Iran: We could not verify fresh October news; oil above $100 still signals supply fear.
  • Warsh: Today's Fed decision isn't confirmed here; Warsh leans hawkish and data-dependent.
  • Week Ahead: Apple and other big earnings next week, a likely jobs report, then CPI on Nov 10.
  • Outlook: Near term neutral; longer term, high rates and oil cap upside.
  • Trades: Favor energy and a steeper yield curve; trim the riskiest junk; wait on gold.

  • Regime Rules: S&P 500 risk-on; NDX risk-on, 6.6% above its sell trigger; trend intact; credit spreads calm

Wednesday's session was quiet on the surface. The S&P 500 rose 0.28% to 7743.98, the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.27% to 26549.85, and the Russell 2000 led with +0.41%. The VIX fell 0.61 to 16.91. Overseas, the Nikkei added 1.08% to 63954.19 and Europe was flat (SX5E +0.05%). Underneath, Treasuries kept steepening. The 2Y fell 3.9bp to 4.6975% while the 10Y rose 2.1bp to 5.0175% and the 30Y rose 3.3bp to 5.3437%. That combination is consistent with the market pricing a Fed that is not tightening near term (the 2Y fell on the day) while demanding more term premium for fiscal and inflation risk: the budget deficit is -6.119% of GDP and WTI is $102.78 (reported +2.88%) with Brent at $114.10. The biggest credit story is high-yield contagion. The Bloomberg Caa–B gap is 792bp, against a 5-year average of ~415bp, at the 99.8th 5-year percentile. It is up 99bp in a month and 245bp in three months, and the FRED ICE CCC series (1,345bp) sits at the 99.9th percentile. So far the rot is NOT spreading up the quality ladder. Single-B (296bp) moved +4bp and Ba (185bp) +5bp over the month, and both actually tightened over the past week (-27bp and -16bp). The B–Ba gap (111bp) is below its 5-year average, and IG (85bp) sits near the 10th all-time percentile. The 63-day Caa/B correlation has risen from 0.35 three months ago to 0.66, but it is still below its 5-year median of 0.70. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal: CCC stress is acute and isolated for now, with the correlation drift the thing to watch. On AI credit, CoreWeave 5Y CDS is ~1,064bp, 131bp below the Oct 15 record and still holding about 82% of its run from the June low. Nvidia CDS is at 125bp. The CDS log has only one day of history, so there is no daily change yet. None of these readings met today's mandatory-discussion triggers. Sentiment is complacent but not euphoric: VIX is low and the AAII bull-bear spread is -8.9. Mega-cap results from Microsoft and Alphabet (scheduled Oct 28) were not verifiable via our news search at publication.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 481.52 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is trading at 481.52 cents/gal, an extreme reading on every gauge: outright price sits at the 99.8th percentile (z 3.25), and the refining crack is at 99.4584 $/bbl (z 5.27). Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.69 vol points (43th percentile of the 54 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 94.5 (68th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 92bp (steeper by 2bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (114bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 27 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

Not at March-2000 conditions on equity froth, but the late-cycle catalyst and signpost dimensions are at or beyond dot-com-peak levels of complacency. Computed: Nasdaq trailing P/E 41.25x is only 16% of the way to the 175x peak, the 200DMA stretch is at 12%, and semis P/E is at 49%. Catalysts are mixed: the yield curve is 68% of the way to 2000 conditions, while IG tightness (129%), Baa–10Y tightness (169%), the VIX (190%), financial conditions (152%) and commodities-vs-equities (200%) are all past the 2000 comparison. PMIs (9–10%), AAII sentiment (27%) and consumer confidence (20%) are far from euphoric. The macro cycle, rather than valuations, looks like a bubble top.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (41x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Today's setup is an expensive market with complacent credit and volatility. It is not a speculative mania in price or sentiment. On the computed chart, the current cycle (anchored Oct-2022) is at month 48 with the index at ~242. In both dot-com analogs, the equivalent point came well before the blow-off: the 1990-anchored panel peaked at month 113, and the 1994-anchored panel at month 69 near 665. The concentration, CAPE, Buffett-indicator, IPO-froth and long-term EPS-growth figures above are analyst estimates. They were not verified by web search in this run because the search budget went to news, so treat them as approximate. High concentration and CAPE plus elevated long-term EPS expectations are the classic BofA signposts that worry us. A 5%+ 10Y yield, a steepening curve and widening CCC spreads are the kind of catalysts that ended prior cycles. The 2000 drawdown reference: Nasdaq -78% over 31 months from the 2000-03-10 peak.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

The Oct 27–28 FOMC outcome could not be confirmed from our search results at publication. Pre-meeting reporting showed markets mostly expected a hold, with one report citing ~15% CME FedWatch odds of a hike. Warsh had named October and December as decision points without prejudging them. Our inference is that today's 3.9bp drop in the 2Y is more consistent with a hold or no hawkish surprise than with a hike. Verify against the official statement.

~1 YEAR

Inference from his on-record remarks: a hawkish-leaning, data-dependent Fed. Warsh has said returning inflation to 2% remains the priority and that inflation is not slowing. His debut June meeting held at 3.50–3.75% and dropped forward guidance, and coverage afterward said hikes were back on the table. Over ~1 year we expect policy to stay restrictive, with at least one more hike plausible if core PCE (3.00759%) and energy pass-through stay hot. Cuts look unlikely unless labor weakens markedly from 4.2% unemployment. Sources disagree on the current funds-rate range (3.50–3.75% vs 3.75–4.00% after September), so we do not assert a level.

Warsh has ended forward guidance and frames each meeting as a fresh decision, which raises the volatility of rate expectations. The next data hurdles are October CPI on Nov 10 and the Dec 8–9 FOMC with new projections; the September SEP reportedly put the year-end median at 4.1%. A 10Y above 5% while the 2Y eases suggests markets trust Warsh on near-term inflation but demand compensation for fiscal and term risk. Flag: the one-year path is our inference, not a Warsh statement.

Sources: investingLive – Warsh won't prejudge rest of 2026, names October and December as decision points · Wealth Professional – Fed rate hike in 2026 now possible after Warsh's debut meeting · investingLive – Warsh rewrites the Fed playbook as FOMC holds rates and signals hikes ahead · Crypto Briefing – Fed's Warsh: Inflation not slowing, 2% target remains priority · MPA – Key dates that will define Kevin Warsh's opening months as Fed chair · iTiger – Markets broadly expect the Fed to hold in October, but Warsh could deliver a surprise
